ZONE: ...a place with a roof... repeat... a roof...
...don't know the name... there's a sign...
SURVIVOR: ...i can hear you sometimes... can you hear me...
TRANSMISSION: ...a message meant for someone in particular...
RARE: ...a far-off broadcast, fading in and out...
...it stops when you get close... then starts again...
...warm, somehow. Like a room with people in it...
TRANSMISSION:MORSE: ...dits and dahs, steady as a heartbeat...
TRANSMISSION:CAESAR: ...letters, read out flat: K. R. O. Z...
TRANSMISSION:TAP: ...tapping on a pipe. Pauses. More tapping...
TRANSMISSION:VIGENERE: ...letters that change their mind every time...
TRANSMISSION:PLAYFAIR: ...a man spells words in NATO, very calm...
TRANSMISSION:NUMBERS: ...a woman reads numbers. A bell. More numbers...
TRANSMISSION:BOOK: ...three numbers at a time, like references...

text: A tango drifts out of the static. Someone has a record player working.
A voice counts numbers. Seven, three, one, nine. Then nothing.
rare.lore: Someone broadcasts numbers on the short band: 7-3-1-9. Always the same voice.

text: An automatic beacon repeats the location of a battery depot. Your assistant writes down what's readable.
An emergency beacon, still on batteries. You take it apart by ear: good for parts.
rare.teaser: ...an emergency beacon, steady as a heartbeat...

text: A recorded weather report from years ago. It promises sun all weekend.
Someone is calling for a woman named Marta. Calling and calling. Nobody answers.
rare.lore: On the medium band, a man calls for Marta every day at the same time.

text: A trucker's CB, left keyed on a dashboard somewhere. Wind, and a radio playing a cumbia under it. You note the landmarks he passes.

rare.teaser: ...this is the municipal hospital... supplies at...
text: A hospital's evacuation notice, still looping. It lists a supply drop that nobody ever collected. Your assistant writes it down.
Two kids on walkie-talkies, years ago or right now, you can't tell. One of them laughs. Then the batteries give out.
Church bells, recorded, played on a schedule by a timer nobody turned off. Someone, once, wanted the city to know what time it was.
An old grain market report. Prices for things nobody sells anymore. At the end, a farm's address and 'we have seed, come trade'.

rare.teaser: ...hum... a generator, close to a mic...
text: A microphone left open next to a running generator. By the pitch, your assistant guesses the model, and how to fix yours.
Someone hums a lullaby into a microphone. It's not for you. It goes on until it stops.
A military net, automated, asking for an authentication nobody remembers. It reads out a depot it still thinks is guarded.
A voice on the frequency says your words from earlier today, in your voice, a little too slow. Then it says them again, slower.
rare.lore: Something on the dial repeated my own transmissions back to me. Slower each time. I haven't told the others.

text: Scratching. Something drags itself across a microphone, slowly, for a full minute. Then it taps twice, as if it knows you're there.
Someone's getting married on the air. Vows, a cheer, a scratchy record for the first dance.
rare.lore: On the medium band, once: a wedding, broadcast so everyone could come.

text: A woman reads out what's in the night sky, planet by planet. 'Saturn's up. Still there. Good.'
Kids singing happy birthday, off-key, to somebody called Nico. Someone blows out candles.
A man describes a lost dog: brown, one white ear, answers to Tango. 'He'll come if you whistle.'
Somebody confesses to the radio, quietly, something they did on the first night. Then: 'Thank you for listening.'
An old radio play: a detective, a storm, a body in the library. Someone does all the voices.
A weather balloon still sending readings. Altitude, pressure, temperature. It's very high up and very alone.
A choir practising scales. Someone keeps getting it wrong. They start again, laughing.
Something long and low on VLF, rising and falling. Whale song, maybe. Or something pretending.
An auction somewhere: a bicycle, a box of candles, a working watch. Bids in chips. Somebody wins the watch.

transmissions.lore: Net MERLIN, from the deep band: Echo-7 relays the Voice. The station is a repeater, not the source.
A numbers station, pad 7: 'the silence was a test'. A test of what, it doesn't say.
A numbers station, pad 19: 'they are listening to you'. Meant for whoever has the pad. You do.

transmissions.lore: A book code against the 1974 handbook: 'the voice lies, do not answer'.

transmissions.text: echo seven is under the dam
transmissions.lore: Book code: 'echo seven is under the dam'. Not the antenna: under the dam.
Way up the short band, in Morse: 'is anyone on this frequency?'. Someone else is sweeping too.
From the deep band, plainly: 'we hear you, bunker'.

stations.name: AUTOMATED WEATHER
stations.lore: AUTOMATED WEATHER (short band): a robot still reading the forecast for the week the Silence began. Sunny, all of it.
lines: Tuesday: sunny, highs of twenty-four. Light wind from the north.
Wednesday: sunny. Good day to hang the washing out.
UV index: high. Remember your hat.
Thursday: sunny. Friday: sunny. Saturday: sunny.
This forecast was updated... [the date is a long beep].
Monday: sunny. Tuesday: sunny. A perfect week for the beach.
Pollen count: high. Allergy sufferers, stay indoors. [a long pause] Everyone, stay indoors.
Sunset at 19:42. Sunrise at... at... [the recording skips] ...sunny.

stations.name: LU3 · OLD BERTO
stations.lore: LU3 · OLD BERTO (short band, 98.40 MHz): a ham who talks about his garden every evening from 19:00 to 20:00. He never answers back. Maybe he can't hear us.
lines: ...the tomatoes came in again. Small, but red. Red is good.
...if anyone's out there, boil the water. Twice. I learned the hard way.
...my wife used to say I talk to the radio more than to her. Well. Now it's just the radio.
...saw a dog today. Thin. I gave it half my bread. Don't tell anyone.
...the antenna's leaning. I'll fix it tomorrow. I say that every day.
...this is LU3, still here, still listening. Over.
...the snails got the lettuce. I'm not angry. Everyone's got to eat.
...planted the beans by the moon, like my father. Laugh if you want.
...rain tonight, I think. My knee says so, and my knee is never wrong.
...the neighbour's cat comes to sit with me while I weed. No neighbour. Still a cat.

stations.name: EMERGENCY BROADCAST
stations.lore: EMERGENCY BROADCAST (short band): the official instructions, looping since day one. Stay inside. Seal the windows. Do not answer.
lines: THIS IS AN EMERGENCY BROADCAST. STAY INSIDE. SEAL DOORS AND WINDOWS.
DO NOT RESPOND TO UNIDENTIFIED VOICES. THEY ARE NOT RESCUE.
RATION WATER. ONE LITER PER PERSON PER DAY.
AUTHORITIES WILL CONTACT YOU. AUTHORITIES WILL CONTACT YOU. AUTHORITIES WILL
...THIS IS NOT A TEST. REMAIN WHERE YOU ARE. HELP IS ON THE WAY...
...the following areas are under curfew until further notice...
...do not drink tap water. Do not open your door to anyone you do not know...

stations.name: RADIO NOSTALGIA
stations.lore: RADIO NOSTALGIA (medium band, 881 kHz): somebody plays tango records from 21:00 to 23:00. Nobody announces the songs.
lines: ...a bandoneon, slow, like breathing...
...an old tango about a neighborhood that doesn't exist anymore...
...the record skips. Someone lifts the needle and sets it back down, carefully...
...a waltz. Somebody, very quietly, is dancing near the microphone...
...a crackling record, a bandoneón, a voice from another century singing about a street corner...
...the needle jumps, finds the groove again, and the violin comes back in...
"Next one's for whoever's dancing alone in the kitchen. I see you."

stations.name: THE LITANY
stations.lore: THE LITANY (medium band): a man reads names of the dead, one by one. He has been reading for years. Some of the names are ours.
lines: ...and Rosa, who went for water. And Julián, who went after her...
...we remember them so the silence doesn't...
...and the family on Calle Ocho, all five, we remember...
...I will read until there is no one left to read. Then I will read myself...
"And the silence fell upon the land, and in the silence, a voice."
"Do not fear the quiet. Fear what speaks in it."
"Seven times I asked. Seven times I was answered. I will not tell you what it said."
deadLines: ...{dead}, who answered the radio, we remember...

stations.lore: Short band, at night only: breathing. Close to the microphone. Whoever it is knows when we're listening.
lines: ...breathing. Slow. Close to the microphone...
...breathing. It stops when you stop moving the dial...
...breathing... then a whisper: 'there you are'...
...breathing... and, far off behind it, your own generator...
...breathing. Slower now. Like someone falling asleep...
...a whisper, too low to make out, then nothing...

stations.lore: Medium band, at night: a child counting, playing hide and seek. Nobody is looking for the child. Or someone is.
lines: ...eight... nine... ten... ready or not...
...mom said don't open the hatch. Mom isn't back yet...
...I can hear you breathing. You're bad at hiding...
...found you. Found you. Found you.
"I counted the stars again. There's one more than yesterday."
"Mum says not to talk on the radio. Mum's asleep."
"Are you real? Say something if you're real."

stations.name: THE VOICE
stations.lore: THE VOICE, long band, 245.0 kHz: seven three one nine, for three minutes on the hour, every hour. It's always been here. We just couldn't reach it.
lines: ...seven. three. one. nine...
...seven. three. one. nine. ... nine. nine...
...seven. three. one. ... we hear you...
...seven. three. one. nine. bunker. bunker. bunker...
"...seven, three, one, nine. Seven, three, one, nine. Acknowledge."
"...seven, three, one, nine. Repeat. Seven..." and then a breath, a human breath.

stations.lore: Deep band: a choir of carriers, all on one frequency, humming the same note. It changes by a hair whenever we transmit.
lines: ...a hundred carriers hum one note...
...the note bends, just a little, when you touch the dial...
...under the hum, a single word, again and again: 'listening'...
...the voices change key together, all at once, as if they'd agreed...
...under the choir, very faintly, the same seven-three-one-nine...

stations.name: RELIEF NET
stations.lore: RELIEF NET (short band, 101.20 MHz): a volunteer reads out where the food was left. 06:00, 14:00 and 22:00, ten minutes each. Be there, or have someone on the radio.
lines: Relief net, morning drop. Two crates under the overpass, blue tarp. Take what you need, leave the crates.
Relief net. Bread's gone hard but it's bread. Bus shelter on the avenue, behind the ad.
Relief net. Canned beans, back of the church. Don't take all of it. Somebody else is hungry too.
Relief net, short one tonight. Rice in the school gym, under the stage. Stay safe.
Relief net. We're running low. Leaving what we can. If you have extra, leave some for others.
Relief net. Water purification tablets left at the old bus shelter on the main road.
Relief net. The church hall is warm tonight. Bring a blanket if you have one.
Relief net. We have a doctor until Thursday. After that, we don't know.

stations.name: SCAV NET
stations.lore: SCAV NET (medium band, 1057 kHz): scavengers swap warnings at 13:00, fifteen minutes. Gruff, fast, useful.
lines: Scav net. Dogs moved north of the tracks. Big pack. Don't be a hero.
Scav net. Somebody rigged wires in the old offices. Watch your feet.
Scav net. Raiders camped by the river. Three, maybe four. Armed.
Scav net. Roof's gone on the hospital's east wing. Don't climb it.
Scav net. Gas leak somewhere downtown. You'll smell it. Turn back.
Scav net. Supermarket on the ring road is bare, don't bother.
Scav net. Somebody's trading fuel for medicine at the Fair. Fair rates, for once.
Scav net. Dogs are back on the east side. More than last week.

stations.name: THE LOCKSMITH
stations.lore: THE LOCKSMITH (medium band, 1606 kHz): five minutes at 03:00 and 15:00. A dry voice reads where things are hidden, then a modem screech. Nobody knows why he shares.
lines: ...under the third floorboard from the window. The key is in the lamp...
...behind the boiler, a false panel. Push, don't pull...
...the safe in the back office opens with the year the factory opened...
...inside the hollow of the fallen tree, wrapped in plastic...
"Under the third bench from the fountain. Loose stone. You're welcome."
"Ticket office at the old station. Behind the timetable board. Mind the glass."

stations.name: DR. LEVY
stations.lore: DR. LEVY (short band, 92.60 MHz): a doctor gives advice every morning at 10:00 for half an hour, and says where she left supplies.
lines: Boil it, then boil it again. And today's kit is in the pharmacy's back door, the one with the red mark.
Clean wounds with what you'd drink, not what you'd fear. Bandages left by the clinic gate.
If it smells sweet, it's infected. Come find me. Or take the antiseptic I left at the bus depot.
Sleep is medicine too. So is the box under the bench at the square.
"Clean water first, then food, then everything else. In that order."
"Fever and a rash? Rest, fluids, and keep them away from the others."
"I left bandages by the library steps. Take what you need, leave what you can."

stations.name: CHAPEL OF SAN ROQUE
stations.lore: CHAPEL OF SAN ROQUE (medium band, 1244 kHz): someone plays the organ every morning at 08:00 for three quarters of an hour. Nobody sings. Nobody has to.
lines: ...an organ, slow, a hymn half the city used to know...
...the same hymn again, a little faster, as if the player is in a hurry today...
...a wrong note. A pause. Then the hymn starts over from the top...
...the hymn finishes, and in the silence someone coughs, and starts it again...
...a different hymn today. Brighter. Someone must have found new sheet music...

stations.lore: Short band, 103.54 MHz, at night only: a music box playing a waltz. When it winds down, someone winds it again. We never hear who.
lines: ...a music box, playing a waltz...
...the waltz slows... slows... and then the key turns, and it starts again...
...the music box, and very close to the microphone, someone humming along, off key...
...the box is wound slower tonight, every note stretched...
...a second music box joins the first, a little out of step...

stations.name: THE FAIR
stations.lore: THE FAIR (short band, 96.40 MHz): a market in the old fairground, on the air 06:00 to noon and 18:00 to midnight. They take chips. Trade from RADIO → TRADE while they're on, then fetch it or pay a courier.
lines: The Fair, the Fair! Batteries in, medicine out. Chips only, no IOUs, no tears.
Fresh in from the coast: tins, rope, a working kettle. Somebody bring me fuel.
Courier leaves at the top of the hour. Pay the runner, not me.
Plans, blueprints, drawings, whatever you call them. Know-how's the only thing that doesn't rot.
We're open, we're armed, we're friendly. In that order.
Lost and found: one dog, answers to Tango. Bring him back, there's chips in it.
Morning crowd's in. Somebody brought eggs. Real eggs. Line forms on the left.
Evening session. Lamps are lit, prices are fair, the guards are awake.
Lost a boot at the Fair? We found eleven. None of them match.
Swap table's open: bring a thing, take a thing. Don't be the one who brings a rock again.

stations.name: LATE PIANO
stations.lore: LATE PIANO (short band, 89.20 MHz), at night only: someone plays an upright piano, badly tuned, the same few pieces. Between them, a cough, a chair, a glass set down.
lines: ...the same piece again. Slower this time, as if they're thinking about someone...
...a wrong note, a laugh, and they start over...
"This one's for Marta. She always said I rushed it."
...the piano stops. A long silence. Then the lid closes, gently...
...somebody hums along, very quietly, from the next room...
"Can't sleep either? Good. Then you can listen."

stations.name: THE PORCH
stations.lore: THE PORCH (medium band, 764 kHz): every evening at 17:00, a man with a guitar on what sounds like a porch. Crickets. He talks between songs to whoever's out there.
lines: "Evening. Sun's going down orange again. That's the dust, they say. Pretty dust."
...an old folk tune, the guitar a little out of tune, his foot keeping time on wood...
"Had a dog come by today. Didn't stay. Nobody stays. That's all right."
"This one my grandmother sang. I don't know the words past the first verse, so you'll get that one twice."
"If you're walking tonight, walk with the moon at your back. Old trick."
...a string breaks mid-song. A long sigh. "Five strings it is, then."

stations.name: THE SOCIAL CLUB
stations.lore: THE SOCIAL CLUB (medium band, 1513 kHz): at 20:00, an hour of accordion from what sounds like an old neighbourhood club. Glasses, chairs scraping, someone who won't stop requesting the same tango.
lines: ...the accordion swells, and somebody at the back shouts for the same tango as last night...
"For the couples. All three of them." Laughter. Shuffling feet.
"The bar's open. The bar's always open. The bar is, technically, a table."
...an old man sings along, half a beat behind, and nobody minds...
"Ten minutes. Then the generator needs a rest, and so do my fingers."
"Same time tomorrow. Bring someone. Bring anyone."

stations.name: BEDTIME STORIES
stations.lore: BEDTIME STORIES (short band, 107.00 MHz): at 22:00, a woman reads a story for half an hour. It's always the same one, about a lighthouse keeper. She never reaches the end.
lines: "Once there was a lighthouse keeper who kept the light burning long after the ships stopped coming."
"Every night he climbed the hundred and twelve steps and lit the lamp, in case."
"In case of what, the gulls asked him. In case, he said. That's all. In case."
"One night a light answered from far out on the water. Just once. Then nothing."
"He kept his light burning, and he waited, and he..." She stops. "That's enough for tonight."
"Sleep, all of you. Someone's keeping the light on."

stations.name: THE MATCH
stations.lore: THE MATCH (medium band, 1138 kHz): every afternoon at 16:00 a man narrates a football match from memory, the final from years ago, play by play. It never ends the same way.
lines: "...the ball out to the wing, he's past one, past two, he looks up... and the stadium holds its breath..."
"Minute sixty-seven. Still nil-nil. My heart can't take this. It didn't then either."
"GOAL! GOOOOAL! ...no. No, wait. Offside. I always forget it was offside."
"The keeper, a giant, a wall, a cathedral of a man, punches it clear!"
"Injury time. The whole country on its feet. And then... I'll tell you tomorrow."
"Today they win. Yesterday they lost. It's my match. I'll call it how I like."

stations.name: BREAKER NINE
stations.lore: BREAKER NINE (long band, 189.0 kHz): a trucker on the long roads, talking to nobody on an old CB, day and night. Road reports, mostly, and stories.
lines: "Breaker nine, breaker nine. Bridge on route five is out. Don't trust the detour signs, they lie."
"Eighty kilometres of nothing. Saw a horse. Just a horse, standing on the road, looking at me."
"Diesel's down to a quarter. Somebody tell me there's a station still pumping out here."
"My kid used to ride up front. Called the white lines 'the zipper'. Still do, in my head."
"Fog on the plateau thick as wool. Going twenty. Going ten. Stopped. Waiting."
"Breaker nine signing off for the night. Somebody keep the road warm."

teasers: ...static... and someone says your name the way {name} did...
heard: {frequency}. A voice that sounds like {name}: "{words}". Then static, and nothing.
{frequency}. For three seconds it's {name}, clear as if {he:name} were in the next room: "{words}". Then it's gone.
{frequency}. {name}'s voice, slowed down, saying "{words}" over and over until the signal drowns it.
echo.lore: Heard on the short band, weeks too late: {name}'s voice. "{words}"
heardPartner: {frequency}. {name}'s voice. Not words for anyone else: your name, the way only {he:name} said it. Then: "{words}"
{frequency}. {name}, very close, as if {he:name} were whispering against your neck: "{words}". The static takes {him:name} back.
